recipe.history:
Muenster cheese — spelled "Munster" in its homeland — traces its origins to the Vosges Mountains of Alsace, a region that has passed between French and German hands so many times it carries both cultures in its bones. The cheese was first crafted by Benedictine monks in the seventh century, who settled in the valley town of Munster and needed a way to preserve the milk of their cows through the long Alpine winters. They developed a washed-rind technique, bathing the aging wheels in brine and sometimes local beer or eau-de-vie, which produced a supple, pale interior with a rust-colored rind and a scent that announced itself boldly before you ever lifted the lid of the cheese box. Authentic Munster d'Alsace carries an AOC designation in France and AOP protection in Europe, meaning only cheese made in the defined Vosges region can legally bear the name. It is a cheese of place, of ritual, and of patience — a product that could only have come from monks who understood that the best things in life require tending.

When Muenster crossed the Atlantic with waves of German and Alsatian immigrants in the nineteenth century, it underwent a quiet, democratic transformation. American dairies — particularly in the Midwest, where those immigrant communities settled thickly — began producing a milder, creamier interpretation that stripped away the pungent washed rind and leaned into the cheese's natural buttery melt. The result was a product purpose-built for American eating: a cheese that melts into a smooth, almost satin blanket at low heat, clings to a patty without greasing out, and delivers a gentle tang that doesn't compete with the beef. By the mid-twentieth century, Muenster had earned a permanent place in the American deli case, sliced thin for sandwiches, layered into casseroles, and eventually, inevitably, draped over a burger patty sizzling on a flat-top grill. Its extraordinary meltability made it a natural fit — a cheese that becomes part of the burger rather than simply sitting on top of it.

I first encountered a Muenster burger at a diner that had no right to be as good as it was — a narrow, linoleum-floored place outside of Albuquerque with a hand-lettered specials board and a cook who had been working the same flat-top since before I was born. My grandfather ordered without looking at the menu. Muenster burger, medium rare, no ketchup. He said it the way people say things they have said a thousand times, and when it arrived I understood why. The cheese had melted into every crevice of the patty, the edges lacy and golden where they'd kissed the griddle, and the whole thing smelled like something between a steakhouse and a childhood kitchen. He slid half across the table to me without being asked. That diner is gone now, and my grandfather too, but every time I cook a Muenster burger I am briefly back in that booth with the sticky laminate table and the smell of rendered beef fat and something right and good about the world.

Medium rare is not a preference — it is the only intellectually defensible endpoint for a beef burger patty, and anyone who tells you otherwise is either misinformed or cooking from fear. At an internal temperature of 130–135°F (54–57°C), the muscle fibers of a freshly ground beef patty have contracted just enough to firm the texture while leaving the interior yielding, juicy, and deeply beefy. The Maillard reaction has done its work on the exterior crust, producing hundreds of flavor compounds that exist nowhere else in the process. Beyond 140°F the myosin proteins tighten irreversibly, moisture evacuates the patty, and you are left with something that requires condiments not to enhance flavor but to compensate for its absence. The argument for cooking a burger to well done is the argument for ironing a linen shirt until it becomes cardboard — technically possible, fundamentally a mistake. Use fresh-ground beef from a trusted source, handle it cold, and trust the thermometer. The burger will reward your confidence with everything a burger is supposed to be.
ingredients: 500g (about 1 lb 2 oz) beef chuck, cut into 1-inch cubes, chilled
150g (about 5 oz) beef short rib meat, cut into 1-inch cubes, chilled
1 tablespoon neutral oil (such as canola or grapeseed) for the griddle
2–3 leaves of green leaf or butter lettuce
300g (2 1/3 cups) bread flour, plus extra for dusting
2 large eggs, room temperature (1 for dough, 1 for egg wash)
60g (4 tbsp) unsalted butter, softened and cubed
1 tablespoon sesame seeds (optional, for topping buns)
instructions: 1. MAKE THE BUNS — ACTIVATE YEAST: Combine the warm water (110°F/43°C), warm milk, sugar, and instant yeast in the bowl of a stand mixer. Stir gently and let stand 5 minutes until foamy.

2. MAKE THE BUNS — MIX DOUGH: Add the bread flour and salt to the yeast mixture. Attach the dough hook and mix on low (speed 2) for 2 minutes until a shaggy dough forms. Add 1 egg and mix on medium (speed 4) for 4 minutes.

3. MAKE THE BUNS — ADD BUTTER: With the mixer running on medium-low, add the softened butter one cube at a time, waiting for each piece to fully incorporate before adding the next. Once all butter is added, increase to medium-high (speed 6) and knead for 8–10 minutes until the dough is smooth, elastic, and pulls cleanly from the bowl sides.
4. MAKE THE BUNS — FIRST RISE: Shape the dough into a ball, place in a lightly oiled bowl, cover with plastic wrap, and let rise at room temperature until doubled in size, about 1 to 1.5 hours.

5. MAKE THE BUNS — SHAPE: Punch down the dough and divide into 4 equal portions (roughly 130g each). Shape each into a tight ball by pulling the surface taut underneath. Place on a parchment-lined baking sheet, spacing at least 3 inches apart. Press each ball gently to flatten slightly into a bun shape.
6. MAKE THE BUNS — SECOND RISE: Cover loosely with oiled plastic wrap and let proof at room temperature until puffy and nearly doubled, about 45–60 minutes.

7. MAKE THE BUNS — BAKE: Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Beat the remaining egg with 1 tablespoon of water for egg wash. Brush the tops of the buns gently and sprinkle with sesame seeds if using. Bake for 16–18 minutes until deep golden brown. Transfer to a wire rack and cool completely before slicing.

8. MAKE THE MAYONNAISE: Whisk the egg yolk, Dijon mustard, and white wine vinegar together in a medium bowl until combined. While whisking constantly, add the neutral oil in a very slow, thin stream — almost drop by drop at first — until the mixture begins to emulsify and thicken. Once stable, add the oil in a slightly faster stream. Whisk in the lemon juice and salt. Taste and adjust seasoning. Refrigerate until needed.

9. GRIND THE BEEF: Pass the cold chuck and short rib cubes through a meat grinder fitted with a coarse die (or pulse in batches in a food processor, keeping the meat very cold). For best texture, grind once through a coarse plate, then once more through a fine plate. Keep the ground beef refrigerated until ready to form patties.

10. FORM THE PATTIES: Divide the ground beef into 2 equal portions (approximately 325g / 11.5 oz each) for thick pub-style patties, or 4 portions for thinner smash-style patties. Handle the meat as little as possible — overworking develops tough texture. Form each portion into a disc roughly 4.5 inches in diameter and 3/4 inch thick. Press a shallow dimple in the center of each patty with your thumb to prevent puffing during cooking. Season generously on both sides with kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper immediately before cooking.
11. HEAT THE COOKING SURFACE: Place a cast-iron skillet or heavy griddle over high heat for 3–4 minutes until it is smoking hot. Add the neutral oil and swirl to coat.

12. COOK THE PATTIES — FIRST SIDE: Place the patties in the pan — do not press down. Cook undisturbed for 3–4 minutes until a deep, mahogany crust has formed and the patty releases easily from the surface.

13. COOK THE PATTIES — FLIP AND MELT CHEESE: Flip each patty once. Immediately lay a slice of Muenster cheese over each patty. Cook for a further 2–3 minutes. Begin checking internal temperature after 2 minutes using an instant-read thermometer inserted into the thickest point of the patty. Pull the patties off the heat at 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare. If desired, tent loosely with a small piece of foil or add a splash of water to the pan and cover briefly to steam-melt the cheese into a smooth, glossy layer.
14. REST THE PATTIES: Transfer patties to a wire rack or plate and rest for 3 minutes. The residual heat will carry the internal temperature a degree or two, and the juices will redistribute.

15. TOAST THE BUNS: While the patties rest, melt the 2 tablespoons of butter in the same skillet over medium heat. Place the buns cut-side down and toast for 60–90 seconds until golden and lightly crisped. Remove and set aside.

16. ASSEMBLE: Spread a generous layer of homemade mayonnaise on the bottom bun. Add the lettuce leaf, then the tomato slice, seasoning the tomato lightly with salt. Place the rested Muenster-topped patty on the tomato. Layer on the thinly sliced white onion and the bread-and-butter pickles. Spread a thin layer of Dijon mustard on the cut face of the top bun. Press the top bun down gently and serve immediately.
